items.title: The cryptography behind electronic voting (and why paper ballots are still essential)
items.summary: As millions of Americans vote in today’s U.S. midterms, most will use paper ballots, which are protected by strict chain-of-custody protocols and, in some cases, statistical audits. You may wonder why we still use paper for our elections and voting systems when tasks like banking, tax filing, and document signing have moved away from paper-based legacy systems and become fully electronic. The short answer: security.That may come as a surprise to some. After all, cryptography and other security advancements have enabled secure electronic systems for many applications. In fact, cryptography can be used to provide two essential safeguards in elections: keeping (1) individual votes secret while (2) making the final tally independently verifiable. This is exactly the approach of cryptographic protocols like Helios and ElectionGuard. However, Helios intentionally targets lower-risk and lower-coercion settings rather than high-stakes public elections. ElectionGuard, by contrast, is intended for public elections, but not as a replacement for a paper-based system; it is used as a cryptographic layer integrated with traditional voting infrastructure.In this blog post, we’ll explain how cryptographic techniques can help protect ballot secrecy and prevent manipulation in electronic voting systems, and explore the limitations of these systems. Although cryptography can strengthen election verifiability and have other strong security properties, it cannot fully replace the security and trust of existing paper ballot systems in general elections.The challenges of electronic votingThe National Academy of Sciences’ excellent 2018 report on election security concludes that electronic ballot return (also known as online voting or internet voting) should not be used in general elections, since “no known technology guarantees the secrecy, security, and verifiability of a marked ballot transmitted over the Internet.”The difficulty of this problem makes sense when you consider the strong security guarantees any election system requires:Voter privacy must be maintained, even if a voter has a financial incentive to disclose their vote to a third party.Ballot integrity must be maintained. This becomes especially challenging in the electronic setting because, in general, the voter does not hold a cryptographic identity and cannot sign their ballot cryptographically. Oh, and the electronic voting client and server may be compromised anyway.Voters shouldn’t be able to vote more than once, but this is hard to verify without associating votes with their voters. This becomes even more challenging electronically when, again, voters often lack a digital cryptographic identity.Everyone should be able to trust (and ideally verify) that the election result correctly reflects the voters’ intent.Paper-based voting systems must solve these problems, too. The first three requirements are typically met through standard physical security measures you see in paper ballot election locations: voters identify themselves to polling workers (preventing multiple votes from one person), are given a ballot without their name on it and a secure location to fill it in (protecting voter privacy), and personally hand their ballot to a polling worker and watch as their ballot is submitted for counting (ballot integrity). As with any security controls, there are threats that can compromise these protections; however, compromising them at a nationwide scale is extremely expensive, difficult, and noisy (i.e., detectable) to election observers, making these controls especially effective for large national elections. The final requirement is the most difficult to achieve for paper-based systems, and voters typically have to trust that election workers compute the final tallies honestly, and that chain-of-custody controls coupled with post-election audits would detect any attempt to compromise the election outcome. Cryptography can be used in conjunction with paper-based systems to help strengthen the trust in this final requirement, using what’s known as end-to-end verifiability, as we will explore later in the post.Electronic systems introduce an existentially dangerous failure mode not present in modern, sensible paper-based systems: a supply-chain or 0-day vulnerability that can scale across many voting machines and jurisdictions could allow one person to single-handedly control and influence the outcome of an election (and, depending on the system and exact vulnerability, possibly while evading detection). In traditional paper-based systems, this risk is sharply constrained by independent physical records and physical security controls.
